title: Capacity trust brief for platform purchasers
body:
Executive summary:

This memo frames a procurement-ready narrative for customers evaluating dedicated inference capacity. The goal: give platform/infra buyers a crisp way to justify a committed Redwood Dedicated purchase that emphasizes measurable reliability, operational isolation, and predictable unit economics. Unlike broad marketing copy, this brief is designed to drop into commercial proposals, procurement decks, and pre-RFP alignment sessions with buyers (platform engineering, procurement, finance).

Key value claims (one-liners buyers use internally):
- Predictable throughput: reserved GPU pools + configurable autoscaling deliver sustained throughput SLAs for production inference workloads.
- Operational isolation: logical and physical isolation options reduce noisy-neighbor risk and simplify compliance posture.
- SLA-backed resiliency: contractual uptime and tail-latency SLAs, plus automated fallbacks, make application SLAs achievable.
- Cost certainty: committed capacity with usage smoothing and transparent overage mechanics lets finance forecast unit costs.

Target buyer personas and questions to answer:
- Platform Engineer / SRE: "How do I guarantee 99th percentile latency under steady and bursty loads?"
- Infrastructure Procurement / IT Procurement: "How do we price and contract capacity without hidden variability?"
- Head of Product / CTO: "If inference is core to our UX, how do we avoid outages from vendor capacity churn?"
- Finance / FP&A: "What is the predictable spend profile and what options exist to curb overage risk?"

Core messaging pillars (short, repeatable lines):
1) Capacity you can sign an SLA on: reserve GPU pools sized to your traffic profile with clear throughput guarantees and latency SLO bands.
2) Isolation you can audit: choose tenant-isolated clusters (physical or VPC-isolated) with dedicated telemetry and KMS integration.
3) Predictable economics: fixed capacity commitments with burst allowances, clear overage rates, and monthly token-level usage exports.
4) Safe degradation: built-in model fallbacks and cross-region routing keep apps online when capacity stress or region outages occur.

Proof points and data to include in buyer materials:
- Throughput example: "Customer X - 1M inference calls/day with 512-token average: reserved 4x A100-equivalent nodes, 99.9% availability, 95th p99 latency under 200ms for token streaming—verified in benchmark report (appendix)."
- Isolation options: "Physical cluster (single-tenant), VPC+private control plane, and dedicated-tenant logical separation—audit logs and KMS available for all variants."
- Failure modes & mitigations: list of automated fallback behaviors (compatible model variant swap, region failover, degraded streaming to chunked responses) and RTO/RPO expectations per plan tier.

Procurement-ready artifacts (copy/paste friendly):
- SLA clause (short): "Vendor will provide 99.9% availability for reserved capacity in a 30-day period. Measured availability excludes scheduled maintenance given 72h prior notice and force majeure. Credits: 5% monthly credit for each 0.1% below target up to 100% of monthly recurring fee."
- Isolation clause (short): "Vendor will provision isolated capacity per Appendix A, with audit trail exports, separate KMS key material, and network boundaries to customer-defined VPCs."
- Throughput acceptance test (short): "Within 30 days of provision, vendor will execute a jointly scoped load test; acceptance criteria: sustained throughput >= committed qps for 1 hour while maintaining p95 latency <= agreed threshold."

Common procurement objections and suggested rebuttals:
- "Why not self-host to control cost?"
  Rebuttal: "Self-hosting shifts significant operational risk and headcount to you: kernel tuning, batching strategies, KV cache invalidation, and capacity forecasting. Redwood’s managed offering transfers that stack while preserving contractual throughput—compare TCO including SRE FTEs and 12–18 month amortized hardware refreshes (appendix model)."
- "How do we avoid vendor lock-in?"
  Rebuttal: "We support model version pinning and model export workflows; in addition, Reserved Capacity contracts include a migration assist package (data extraction scripts, baseline model artifacts) to reduce migration friction."
- "What happens during large bursts?"
  Rebuttal: "Committed capacity includes configurable burst pools and automatic throttling with graceful degradation policies; purchase tiers can include predictable burst allowances and priority queueing backed by credits instead of opaque throttles."

Negotiation levers to offer (for AE/CS):
- Trial bridge: short-term committed minimum (90 days) convertible to annual contract credit if upsold.
- Hybrid commit: combine baseline reserved capacity + metered overflow at a pre-negotiated rate.
- SLA escalations: faster incident response or named escalation paths for higher-tier customers.
- Observability add-ons: extended retention for token-level traces and minute-granularity cost dashboards as purchasable line items.

Competitive differentiation (concise bullets):
- vs large cloud provider managed endpoints: Redwood’s runtime and kernel selection are tuned for LLM inference patterns (KV cache, prefix caching, batching) and include fallbacks across model variants—cloud endpoints often lack inference-specific caching and predictable-throughput SLAs.
- vs self-hosted OSS stacks: Redwood takes on ops burden (kernel selection, benchmarking, quantization recommendations), reducing time-to-stable-production and SRE headcount needs.
- vs other inference vendors: highlight unified API across hosted/dedicated/private modes and procurement-friendly legal/contract frameworks designed for regulated enterprises.

Metrics buyers use to approve spend (examples to show in one-pagers):
- p95/p99 token latency under committed throughput
- sustained qps per committed node (and conversion to RPS for typical prompt length)
- monthly MRR vs expected variable spend (forecasted 12-month burn)
- incident MTTR for capacity-related outages

Packaging suggestions for sales motions:
- Platform Starter (90d): baseline reserved capacity for early-stage platform teams, 2-week go-live SLA, 30% volume discount on first quarter.
- Production Reserve (12m): annual committed capacity with 99.9% availability, 24/7 incident support, one acceptance test window, fixed overage rate.
- Enterprise Isolated (12m+): physical cluster or private deployment option, SOC/ISO compliance add-ons, named technical account team, custom SLA and indemnities.

Sample next steps for Sales/AE during procurement calls:
1) Align on buyer persona and their must-have SLA metrics (latency p95/p99, availability).
2) Propose initial committed sizing (based on estimated QPS/token lengths) and a 90-day bridge if needed.
3) Share acceptance test plan and sample SLA language.
4) Offer migration/exit assistance to mitigate lock-in concerns.

Appendix (brief pointers for technical collateral to attach):
- Benchmark report: sustained throughput tests by model family and token length.
- Runbook excerpt: capacity failover flows and escalation ladder.
- TCO model: comparative spreadsheet contrasting managed reserved capacity vs self-hosted with FTE assumptions.

Author note:
This brief is intentionally concise so it can be dropped verbatim into buyer-facing decks and procurement responses. Use the appendices to surface technical evidence—buyers want measurable, testable guarantees, not only marketing claims.

End of memo.
